title: US Missile Stockpiles Hit Critical Lows as Iran War Drags On
excerpt: Analysts warn America has burned through up to 61% of its Patriot missiles and 80% of THAAD interceptors, raising questions about the Pentagon’s ability to sustain prolonged operations — and its readiness for threats elsewhere.
body:
• The US has expended more than 3,000 Tomahawk, Patriot, and JASSM missiles since Operation Epic Fury began in February, according to CSIS estimates.
  • Between 45% and 61% of America’s Patriot missile stockpile and up to 80% of its THAAD interceptors have been used, with full replenishment expected to take years.
  • Defense analysts warn that depleted inventories create a “window of vulnerability” for potential conflicts in the Western Pacific, including over Taiwan.
  • The munitions shortfall could also affect US defense commitments to allies, including India, which relies on American-made systems for its own missile defense.

The United States has burned through a substantial portion of its most advanced missile stockpiles five months into its war with Iran, with defense analysts warning that Washington may not have the munitions to sustain a prolonged escalation — or respond to new threats elsewhere.

An April report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that the US has expended between 45% and 61% of its Patriot missile inventory since Operation Epic Fury began on February 28 — between 1,060 and 1,430 of the 2,330 missiles in its pre-war stockpile. The picture is starker for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system: between 52% and 80% of those interceptors have been used, according to the same report.

Combined with the more than 3,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles and Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSMs) fired at Iranian targets, the depletion marks the largest drawdown of American precision munitions since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Production Cannot Keep Pace

The core problem, analysts say, is that the US defense industrial base cannot produce missiles anywhere close to the rate at which they are being consumed. Patriot missiles currently have an average delivery time of 42 months, according to CSIS. Lockheed Martin signed a deal with the Pentagon in January to increase annual Patriot production from roughly 600 to 2,000 units, but the new capacity will take years to come online.

“Many bottlenecks exist, including shortages of key critical minerals, motors, and advanced electronics,” Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “Money is not a quick fix — it can only work over long periods of time.”

Kavanagh estimated that full replenishment of key stockpiles could take five to ten years, even with existing contracts.

A Window of Vulnerability

While the CSIS assessment concluded that the US “has enough munitions for any plausible scenario in the Iran war,” it warned that depleted inventories have “created a window of vulnerability for a potential Western Pacific conflict” — a reference to the possibility of Chinese military action against Taiwan.

That assessment, however, was made in April. The situation has worsened since, with nine consecutive nights of US airstrikes against Iran and continued Iranian retaliatory attacks. Saturday’s deadly strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, which killed two US service members and injured dozens more, underscored Iran’s ability to penetrate American defenses.

“The attacks make it clear that the size of our presence in the Middle East has become more of a liability,” Katherine Thompson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, told the New York Post. “I don’t think our munitions are in a great place if this lasts another year or two.”

A senior US official told the Washington Post that the Pentagon is planning for a wider war but cautioned: “We do not have enough to safely sustain operations, and I don’t think the White House is aware of that.”

Ripple Effects for Allies

The munitions crunch extends beyond America’s own forces. Eighteen countries use the Patriot system, and the US faces difficult decisions about allocating scarce production among allies under threat — including Gulf states seeking to replenish their own depleted stocks and Ukraine, which continues to battle Russia.

“The U.S. will need to deliver some munitions to allies either under attack or under a threat of attack,” said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS. “Other countries might be pushed back in the queue or receive partial deliveries as the U.S. rebuilds its inventories.”

For India, the implications are direct. New Delhi has invested heavily in US-origin defense systems, including a $3.5 billion order for the MH-60R Seahawk helicopter and ongoing discussions about THAAD-class missile defense acquisitions. A prolonged American production bottleneck could delay deliveries and push India to accelerate its own indigenous defense manufacturing under the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.

What Comes Next

The White House is urging Congress to approve a $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget and has invoked the Defense Production Act to clear regulatory obstacles for defense manufacturing. President Trump has announced $10 billion in private investment commitments for the defense sector and visited a Defense and Innovation Summit in Pennsylvania last week.

But experts say the fundamental constraint is time, not money. Despite ground-breaking ceremonies for new Lockheed Martin munitions plants in Arkansas and at its existing facilities, the lag between investment and output means the US military will operate with diminished stockpiles well into the end of the decade.

With 17 American service members killed since February and roughly 50,000 troops stationed across the Middle East, the debate over whether the US can sustain its current pace of operations is no longer hypothetical.
